finding.claim: dropTable discards the error returned by Authorize, so the dba role check is never enforced. Any caller can run the DROP TABLE statement.
finding.source: Any HTTP client that reaches /admin/drop, including one with no dba role.
finding.sink: runSQL("DROP TABLE " + r.FormValue("t")) at api.go:27, a destructive admin operation.

trace.note: /admin/drop is registered directly to dropTable with no auth middleware.
u is taken from the request context.
Authorize(u, "dba") returns an error for non-dba users, but the return value is ignored.
Execution continues to runSQL with the attacker-chosen table name.

finding.guards_checked: The role check in Authorize is correct, and vacuum at api.go:33-36 handles its error properly. dropTable has no other guard. No middleware is registered in main. The context user is assumed to be set upstream.

verdict.guard_found: Authorize (api.go:13-20) returns an error correctly, but dropTable calls it as a bare statement at api.go:26 and discards the result. No middleware is registered (api.go:44). The only other control is the unchecked type assertion in userFrom (api.go:22), which panics if no user is in the context. That is a crash, not an authorization check.
verdict.reason: api.go:26 discards the error from Authorize, so api.go:27 runs the DROP TABLE with the attacker-controlled `t` for any user who has a context user (e.g. one without the dba role), while vacuum at api.go:33-36 checks the error. Caveat: nothing in this file sets the "user" context value, so if no upstream middleware does, userFrom panics at api.go:22 before the sink. The finding assumes the middleware exists, and it is unconfirmed here.

verdict_facts.guard_found: Authorize(u, "dba") at api.go:26 returns an error, but the result is discarded. There is no middleware, and the handler is registered directly at api.go:44.
verdict_facts.reason: api.go:26 calls Authorize as a bare statement and ignores the returned error, so any authenticated non-dba user reaches the concatenated DROP TABLE at api.go:27. The sibling handler vacuum checks the error at api.go:33-36, which shows the check was intended.

finding.claim: SQL injection: the form value t is concatenated into a DROP TABLE statement with no validation or identifier quoting. The authorization bypass in F1 lets an unprivileged caller reach it. Even a legitimate dba could inject extra statements.
finding.source: r.FormValue("t"), the form or query parameter t on /admin/drop.
finding.sink: runSQL("DROP TABLE " + t) at api.go:27. runSQL is a stub here, but it is the SQL execution point.

trace.note: r.FormValue("t") is concatenated into the SQL string.
runSQL takes the raw string. Nothing here shows parameterization or an allowlist.

finding.guards_checked: There is no allowlist, no identifier validation and no quoting. Table names cannot be bound as query parameters. The only control is the role check, which is bypassed (F1).

verdict.guard_found: Authorize(u, "dba") at api.go:26 returns an error, but the result is discarded as a bare statement, so it blocks nothing. There is no allowlist, quoting or validation of t.
verdict.reason: api.go:27 concatenates r.FormValue("t") into "DROP TABLE " and passes it to runSQL (declared at api.go:41, a stub that is the execution point). The only guard, Authorize at api.go:26, has its error ignored, unlike vacuum at api.go:33, so any caller who passes userFrom (any authenticated user) reaches the sink.

verdict_facts.guard_found: Authorize(u, "dba") at api.go:26 is a bare statement whose error is discarded, so it does not block anything. There is no allowlist, quoting or validation of t.
verdict_facts.reason: api.go:26 discards the error from Authorize, so any authenticated user reaches api.go:27, where r.FormValue("t") is concatenated into "DROP TABLE " + t with no validation or quoting, and runSQL (api.go:41) takes the raw string.

finding.claim: userFrom does an unchecked type assertion on the context value. If no upstream middleware set "user", the assertion panics. net/http recovers the panic per request, so the effect is a failed request rather than a crash. Treat this as a robustness issue, and as a fail-open risk if the surrounding code ever recovers and continues.
finding.source: Any request that arrives without the "user" context value set, for example because auth middleware is absent or bypassed.
finding.sink: r.Context().Value("user").(*User) at api.go:22, which panics on a nil interface.

trace.note: Handlers are registered with no middleware, so nothing in this file sets the context value.
The single-value type assertion panics when the value is nil.

finding.guards_checked: There is no comma-ok check. The authenticating middleware, if any, is outside this file. net/http's per-connection panic recovery limits the impact to the one request.

verdict.guard_found: none (no comma-ok check, no middleware setting "user"; only net/http per-request panic recovery limits impact)
verdict.reason: api.go:22 does an unchecked `.(*User)` assertion, and api.go:44-45 register handlers with no middleware, so nothing sets "user" and an anonymous request panics. The panic is recovered per request by net/http, so this is a low-severity robustness issue. It currently fails closed, because the panic comes before runSQL at api.go:27 and api.go:37. Separate from this finding, api.go:26 discards the result of Authorize, which would be a real authorization bypass once the "user" value is set.

verdict_facts.guard_found: Upstream trusted middleware sets the "user" context value (per project facts). net/http recovers handler panics per request, and no code here recovers and continues.
verdict_facts.reason: The trace is accurate (api.go:22 is a single-value assertion, api.go:44 registers handlers with no middleware), but upstream middleware sets "user" and a missing value panics before any handler effect at api.go:25-27 and api.go:32-37, so the request fails closed with no exploitable impact. The real bug is separate: dropTable discards the Authorize result at api.go:26.
